title: Unified Osculator: Merging Positive and Negative Cases
content:
This file answers an open question from the parent entry `divisibility-truncation-general`: can the positive and negative osculator theorems be merged into a single theorem with a signed osculator $c \in \mathbb{Z}$?

The answer is YES. The key insight is that the condition $d | (10c - 1)$ for positive osculators ($c > 0$) and $d | (10c_{\text{neg}} + 1)$ for negative osculators are the same condition with $c$ replaced by $-c_{\text{neg}}$, since $10(-c_{\text{neg}}) - 1 = -(10c_{\text{neg}} + 1)$.

This gives a single **Unified Osculator Theorem** that subsumes both cases, simplifying the proof architecture from two separate theorems to one plus a sign-conversion corollary.
mathContext: Unification: $d | (10c_{\text{neg}} + 1) \iff d | (10(-c_{\text{neg}}) - 1)$, so the negative osculator rule is the positive rule with $c \mapsto -c_{\text{neg}}$.

title: The Division-Modulus Identity
content: The private helper lemma `div_mod_cast` establishes the fundamental arithmetic identity $(n : \mathbb{Z}) = 10 \cdot \lfloor n/10 \rfloor + (n \bmod 10)$ by casting `Nat.div_add_mod` to integers. This identity is the algebraic engine of the entire proof: multiplying the osculator expression by 10 and substituting this identity produces a term where the (10c-1) factor can be isolated. The proof is a one-liner using `push_cast` (to handle the ℕ → ℤ coercion) and `omega` (to verify the linear arithmetic).
mathContext: $(n : \mathbb{Z}) = 10 \cdot \lfloor n/10 \rfloor + (n \bmod 10)$; fundamental to $10(q + c \cdot r) = n + (10c-1)r$

title: Unified Osculator Theorem
content:
The single theorem that subsumes both positive and negative osculator rules:

```lean
theorem unified_osculator (d : N) (c : Z) (n : N)
    (hcop : IsCoprime (d : Z) 10)
    (hc : (d : Z) | 10 * c - 1) :
    (d : Z) | n <-> (d : Z) | (n/10 + c * (n%10))
```

For $c > 0$ this gives the positive osculator ("add $c$ times the last digit").
For $c < 0$ this gives the negative osculator ("subtract $|c|$ times the last digit").

The proof uses the identity $10 \cdot (n/10 + c \cdot (n\%10)) = n + (10c-1) \cdot (n\%10)$.

title: Negative Osculator as Corollary
content:
The negative osculator rule is a one-line corollary of the unified theorem:

```lean
theorem neg_osculator_from_unified (d : N) (c : Z) (n : N)
    (hcop : IsCoprime (d : Z) 10)
    (hc : (d : Z) | 10 * c + 1) :
    (d : Z) | n <-> (d : Z) | (n/10 - c * (n%10))
```

The proof converts $d | (10c+1)$ to $d | (10(-c)-1)$ and applies the unified theorem with osculator $-c$.

title: Concrete Divisibility Rules
content:
All five classical rules recovered from the unified framework:

| Divisor | Osculator | Type | Rule |
|---------|-----------|------|------|
| 7 | c=-2 | negative | $7|n \iff 7|(n/10 - 2(n\%10))$ |
| 11 | c=-1 | negative | $11|n \iff 11|(n/10 - (n\%10))$ |
| 13 | c=4 | positive | $13|n \iff 13|(n/10 + 4(n\%10))$ |
| 17 | c=-5 | negative | $17|n \iff 17|(n/10 - 5(n\%10))$ |
| 19 | c=2 | positive | $19|n \iff 19|(n/10 + 2(n\%10))$ |

Each instantiation requires two proof obligations: coprimality of $d$ with 10 (discharged by `decide`) and the osculator condition $d | (10c \pm 1)$ (discharged by providing the explicit witness via `norm_num`). The alternation between positive and negative osculators depends on whether $10^{-1} \bmod d$ or $-(10^{-1}) \bmod d$ gives the smaller absolute value.
mathContext: $c_+ = 10^{-1} \bmod d$; whether to use $+c$ or $-c$ depends on which gives a smaller multiplier

title: Dual Osculator Sum Theorem
content:
For any $d$ coprime to 10, the positive osculator $c_+$ and negative osculator $c_-$ satisfy $d | (c_+ + c_-)$.

This follows from $10c_+ \equiv 1$ and $10c_- \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$, so $10(c_+ + c_-) \equiv 0 \pmod{d}$, and coprimality gives $d | (c_+ + c_-)$.

For minimal osculators, $c_+ + c_- = d$ (e.g., 5+2=7, 4+9=13, 12+5=17).

title: Verification Examples and API Summary
content:
Three verification examples confirm the dual osculator sum theorem: $5 + 2 = 7$ for $d = 7$, $4 + 9 = 13$ for $d = 13$, and $12 + 5 = 17$ for $d = 17$. Each is discharged by providing the explicit quotient witness via `norm_num`.

Sanity checks verify divisibility with `native_decide`: $7 | 49$, $13 | 169$, $19 | 57$, and $\neg(7 | 50)$. The `#check` commands confirm the three main theorems are accessible: `unified_osculator`, `neg_osculator_from_unified`, and `dual_osculators_sum`.
